routes.description: Establish the four claimed historical facts from early Christian materials, connect them as a cumulative evidential set, and show that divine resurrection explains that set more adequately than the proposed literary, visionary, or sociological alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources warrant burial, an empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples’ resurrection belief, and if God raising Jesus provides the best comparative explanation of those facts despite objections from historical analogy and source criticism.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest Christian sources establish all four specified facts and that God raising Jesus best explains their conjunction.

centralBridges.description: Establish an identifiable burial and the subsequent discovery of an empty tomb from sufficiently early, independent, and historically credible traditions.
Establish that individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus after his death using authentic early testimony and historically usable narrative sources.
Explain why the earliest disciples sincerely adopted a specific resurrection belief despite the crucifixion and the surrounding Jewish expectations.
Demonstrate comparatively that divine resurrection accounts for the combined evidence better than legendary development, cultural borrowing, visions, or belief-preservation mechanisms.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the authenticity, early dating, and historical admissibility of Pauline traditions and the relevant Gospel materials.
Show that proposed pagan and hero-story parallels lack the relevant similarity or causal connection needed to explain the earliest Christian claims.

routes.description: Deny that the surviving sources warrant the four asserted facts or the resurrection inference by applying historical analogy, literary and textual criticism, and ordinary mechanisms for visionary reports, legendary narratives, and the persistence of religious belief.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if material uncertainty remains about one or more foundational facts, or if familiar literary, cultural, visionary, or sociological processes provide sufficient alternatives to prevent divine resurrection from being established as the best historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest sources do not establish the complete factual conjunction or do not make divine resurrection its best historical explanation.

centralBridges.description: Show that the burial, empty-tomb, and appearance materials are literary, redactional, or textually uncertain enough that the asserted events are not established.
Use comparable ancient vanished-body, apotheosis, dying-and-rising, and appearance narratives to support a legendary or hagiographic account of the traditions.
Provide non-resurrection pathways for exaltation, appearance reports, and continuing faith, including visions, retrojection, syncretism, and cognitive-dissonance reduction.
Show that invoking divine action does not resolve uncertain historical claims or outperform ordinary explanations under a case-by-case evidential method.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend historical ideal-type comparison as requiring meaningful structural similarity rather than exact correspondence or direct literary copying.
Limit the evidential reach of Pauline authenticity claims, later disciple traditions, scholarly consensus, and extra-biblical notices.

sections.title: Source Proximity, Textual Integrity, and Historical Method
sections.rationale: The motion depends on whether Pauline and Gospel materials can function as early historical evidence. This section covers their dating, textual integrity, literary character, admissibility, and the role of analogy in evaluating extraordinary ancient claims.

sections.title: Burial Tradition and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: A known burial place and the subsequent absence of Jesus’ body form a linked evidential foundation for the bodily-resurrection case, while source criticism and alternative literary explanations contest whether either event is historically established.

sections.title: Nature and Historical Status of the Postmortem Appearances
sections.rationale: The reported experiences of individuals and groups are a principal fact asserted by the motion. Their provenance, visionary or bodily character, and relationship to comparable ancient narratives determine what they can establish historically.

sections.title: Origins of the Disciples’ Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: The debate must explain why resurrection belief arose and persisted among Jesus’ followers. Jewish expectations and claimed transformation bear on one account, while syncretism, belief development, and cognitive dissonance supply competing mechanisms.

sections.title: Resurrection as the Best Explanation
sections.rationale: Even if some underlying facts are granted, the motion requires a comparative inference to divine resurrection. This section addresses explanatory adequacy, prior probability, the likelihood of the evidence under alternatives, and whether miraculous agency completes that inference.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Jesus received an honorable burial by Joseph of Arimathea in a known tomb, supported by early Pauline and Markan material and the absence of a rival burial tradition.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Women discovered Jesus' tomb empty on the Sunday after the crucifixion, as supported by Pauline implications, early Markan material, narrative simplicity, and an early hostile explanation presupposing a missing body.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Multiple individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus alive after his death, as indicated by Paul's early witness list, his acquaintance with participants, and multiple Gospel strands.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: The original disciples suddenly and sincerely believed Jesus had risen despite a crucified messiah's apparent failure, the stigma of divine curse, and Jewish expectation of a general end-time resurrection.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: God raising Jesus from the dead best explains the burial, empty tomb, appearances, and origin of resurrection belief because the rejected theft and apparent-death theories do not plausibly explain the cumulative facts.

chunk-001:c010.proposition: Greco-Roman hero and dying-god stories do not explain the original disciples' resurrection belief because their categories differ from Jewish resurrection and no plausible causal route to Galilean disciples is shown.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: First Corinthians 15:3–11 is authentic rather than interpolated because all manuscripts contain it, early writers cite it, its vocabulary and pronouns fit the context, and its removal damages Paul's argument.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-02.proposition: New Testament writings should be evaluated as separate first-century historical documents rather than collectively disqualified because the church later assembled them into a canon.

chunk-005:chunk-005-candidate-001.proposition: Assessing resurrection requires considering not only prior improbability but also how unlikely the empty tomb, appearances, and disciples' faith would be if no resurrection occurred.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Critical historians can assess individual miracle reports without either rejecting every supernatural claim in advance or accepting every reported miracle.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: Historical inference depends on analogy between past and present experience, so familiar legendary explanations may be preferred without metaphysically denying miracles.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: The empty-tomb narrative belongs to a familiar ancient hero-story pattern involving vanished remains, heavenly ascent, appearances, and initial disciple skepticism.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-03.proposition: First Corinthians 15:3–11 is plausibly a later composite creed whose tensions and institutional features weaken its value as early evidence for resurrection appearances.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-05.proposition: Resurrection belief could have arisen by retrojecting an expected future return of Jesus into the past as prior appearances, leaving multiple historical possibilities open.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-06.proposition: Even if a resurrection is conceivable, extant narratives characterized as literary creations do not provide adequate historical evidence for confidence that it occurred.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-07.proposition: The burial and empty-tomb accounts are not established facts because their narrative sources are historically problematic and alternative literary explanations remain available.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-08.proposition: Gospel appearance accounts have limited historical value because visions of Jesus are common and the narratives contain redactional and legendary material.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-09.proposition: The Jesus movement's continuation can be explained through cognitive-dissonance reduction and reinterpretation of disconfirmation without positing a resurrection experience.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-10.proposition: Invoking a miracle does not explain uncertain historical events because it replaces the disputed event with an even less understood causal claim.
